title: What is a consumer group, and how does partition assignment work within and across groups?
shortTitle: Consumer groups and partition assignment within and across groups

s1_definition.profdef: A consumer group is a set of consumer instances that share the same group id and cooperate to consume a topic's partitions. Within a single group, Kafka distributes the topic's partitions so that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer, giving scalable parallel processing where each record is processed once by the group. Across different groups, each group independently receives the full set of partitions, so every group sees every record. The group coordinator on a broker performs the assignment using a configurable partition assignment strategy, and it reassigns partitions whenever consumers join or leave.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a consumer group as a team of clerks at National Bank of India who share one job, such as processing transactions. The team lead (group coordinator) hands each clerk a set of ledger drawers (partitions) so no two clerks on the same team touch the same drawer, and together they get through all the work once. A different team, say the fraud team, has its own lead and its own copy of all the drawers to read independently. Same records, two teams, each doing their own job without stepping on each other.
s1_definition.oneliner: Within a group, partitions are divided so each is owned by one consumer; across groups, every group gets all partitions independently.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A consumer group is a set of consumer instances that share the same group id and cooperate to consume a topic's partitions. Within a single group, Kafka distributes the topic's partitions so that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer, giving scalable parallel processing where each record is processed once by the group. Across different groups, each group independently receives the full set of partitions, so every group sees every record. The group coordinator on a broker performs the assignment using a configurable partition assignment strategy, and it reassigns partitions whenever consumers join or leave.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a consumer group as a team of clerks at National Bank of India who share one job, such as processing transactions. The team lead (group coordinator) hands each clerk a set of ledger drawers (partitions) so no two clerks on the same team touch the same drawer, and together they get through all the work once. A different team, say the fraud team, has its own lead and its own copy of all the drawers to read independently. Same records, two teams, each doing their own job without stepping on each other.

**One line to remember:** Within a group, partitions are divided so each is owned by one consumer; across groups, every group gets all partitions independently.

sections.s2_technical:
A consumer group is identified by its group id, set with `group.id` or in Spring by `spring.kafka.consumer.group-id`. All consumers with the same group id belong to one group and cooperate. The purpose is load sharing: if a topic has twelve partitions and the group has four consumers, Kafka gives each consumer three partitions, so the group processes four times faster than a single consumer while still processing each record exactly once within that group.

Assignment within a group is performed by the group coordinator, a broker role, together with a group leader, which is one of the consumers chosen to compute the assignment. The actual division follows a partition assignment strategy. The RangeAssignor assigns contiguous ranges of partitions per topic, which can cause imbalance across multiple topics. The RoundRobinAssignor spreads partitions evenly one by one. The StickyAssignor and the CooperativeStickyAssignor aim to keep assignments stable across rebalances, moving as few partitions as possible, and the cooperative variant allows incremental rebalancing without stopping all consumers at once. You set this with `partition.assignment.strategy`.

The core invariant within a group is one partition to one consumer. A partition is never shared by two consumers in the same group at the same instant. If there are more consumers than partitions, the surplus consumers get nothing and stay idle, which means you cannot scale a group beyond the partition count. If there are fewer consumers than partitions, some consumers own multiple partitions.

Across groups, assignment is completely independent. Each group has its own group id, its own coordinator state, and its own committed offsets stored in the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic keyed by group id. So the audit group and the fraud group each receive all twelve partitions and each track their own progress. One group falling behind or replaying from an old offset has zero effect on another group. This is how Kafka supports the publish-subscribe pattern: add a new group and it independently consumes the whole topic.

When the group membership changes — a consumer starts, crashes, or is added for scaling — the coordinator triggers a rebalance and recomputes the assignment. During a classic eager rebalance, all consumers briefly stop, give up their partitions, and receive new assignments, which causes a short pause. Cooperative rebalancing reduces this by only revoking the partitions that actually need to move. Consumers prove they are alive with periodic heartbeats; if a consumer misses heartbeats beyond `session.timeout.ms`, the coordinator considers it dead and reassigns its partitions.

The senior-level nuance is capacity planning and offset management. Because a group cannot have more active consumers than partitions, you size partitions for your target parallelism, often with headroom. You also decide the offset commit strategy per group: auto-commit is simplest but risks reprocessing or loss on crashes, while manual commit after processing gives at-least-once semantics with controlled reprocessing. Monitoring consumer lag per group per partition tells you whether a group is keeping up.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must process a transaction stream with a scalable main team and let several other teams read the same stream for their own purposes.

Problem 1 — The main transaction-processing service must share the work across several instances so it keeps up at peak, and each transaction must be processed only once by the team. This is exactly a single consumer group with several consumers, where Kafka divides the partitions so each is owned by one instance.

Problem 2 — The fraud team and the analytics team each need every transaction, independently, without slowing down the main processor. This is exactly multiple consumer groups, where each group gets all partitions and its own offsets.

Problem 3 — When one main-processor instance crashes, its partitions must be picked up by the surviving instances automatically. This is exactly a rebalance within the group triggered by the coordinator.

The mini-project simulates group behavior. We build a `TxnRecord` domain object, a `Topic` with several partitions, a `Coordinator` that assigns partitions within a group using round-robin and handles a consumer leaving, and a `Group` abstraction so we can run a main group and a fraud group. The demo shows the main group dividing partitions among three consumers, a crash causing reassignment, and the fraud group independently reading all partitions.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the topic transactions with 6 partitions, a main group with three instances, and a fraud group with two instances.

Step 1 — The topic is created with 6 partitions. Two sample records are produced and routed to partitions by key, but the focus here is assignment, not the records themselves.

Step 2 — The main group adds three consumers: inst-A, inst-B, inst-C. The coordinator runs round-robin assignment over 6 partitions, giving inst-A partitions 0 and 3, inst-B partitions 1 and 4, inst-C partitions 2 and 5. Each partition has exactly one owner, so the group processes every record once in parallel across three instances.

Step 3 — inst-B crashes. The coordinator detects the missing member and triggers a rebalance. It recomputes the assignment for the two surviving consumers over 6 partitions, giving inst-A partitions 0, 2, 4 and inst-C partitions 1, 3, 5. The crashed instance's partitions were seamlessly picked up, so no work is lost.

Step 4 — The fraud group, a completely separate group, adds two consumers: fraud-1 and fraud-2. Its coordinator assigns all 6 partitions across these two, giving fraud-1 partitions 0, 2, 4 and fraud-2 partitions 1, 3, 5. The fraud group reads every record independently with its own offsets.

Step 5 — The logs show both groups owning the full set of partitions independently, and the main group recovering from a crash by reassigning partitions, demonstrating assignment within and across groups.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A consumer group is a set of consumer instances that share the same group id and cooperate to consume a topic. The key idea is that within a single group, Kafka divides the topic's partitions so that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer. This gives horizontal scaling where the group processes each record once but spreads the work across instances. If a topic has six partitions and the group has three consumers, each consumer gets two partitions, so the group runs three times faster than a single consumer.

Assignment within a group is handled by the group coordinator on a broker, using a configurable strategy such as round-robin, range, or the cooperative-sticky assignor that minimizes partition movement during rebalances. The firm rule is one partition to one consumer within a group, so you cannot have more active consumers than partitions; any surplus consumers sit idle. When a consumer joins, crashes, or is added, the coordinator triggers a rebalance and recomputes the assignment, and the surviving consumers pick up the orphaned partitions automatically.

Across groups, assignment is completely independent. Each group has its own group id, its own coordinator state, and its own committed offsets stored by group id, so every group receives all partitions and reads every record. This is exactly how Kafka supports publish-subscribe: you add a new group and it independently consumes the whole topic without affecting anyone else.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, the main transaction processor runs as one consumer group with several instances that share the partitions, so a crash of one instance triggers a rebalance and the others take over without losing work. The fraud team and the analytics team each run as separate groups, so they independently read every transaction with their own offsets and never slow down the main processor. The senior point I stress is capacity planning: because a group cannot scale beyond the partition count, I size partitions for my target parallelism with headroom, and I monitor consumer lag per group per partition to know whether each team is keeping up.

---

keyPoints: Consumer group: set of consumers sharing topic partitions
Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group
Rebalancing: partition reassignment when consumers join/leave
